articles.title_zh: The Major Social Media Platforms Are All Rejecting Paid Ads for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ (Exclusive)
articles.content_orig:
Senior Editor, Technology and Politics
So much for free speech. The studio releasing Alex Gibney ’s new Elon Musk documentary Musk is finding itself unable to buy an ad on the biggest social platforms. YouTube , TikTok , and Instagram and Facebook owner Meta are all declining to run the trailer for Musk , along with X itself, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. That last one is perhaps understandable, given its owner. But the rejection by the other platforms has taken distributor Bleecker Street by surprise, and it is internally scrambling to understand why the ad has been rejected, according to a person familiar with the company’s processes who is not authorized to talk about them publicly. The unwillingness of platforms to accept even paid advertising is sure to raise concerns about free speech and the dwindling number of companies that control many of the platforms in this country — and ironically provide a proof-text for the very point the film is coming to make. Gibney’s doc is a four-hour look at a title character who attempts to control the conversation in various ways , including with alleged suppressions on X, which he bought in 2022.
Bleecker Street opens Musk in theaters on Oct. 9. YouTube, TikTok and Meta have all supplied a reason related to “political content” to Bleecker Street reps. The latter two companies’ platforms, by policy, do not allow campaign or other political ads, in Meta’s case largely owing to fallout from the Cambridge Analytica Facebook scandal during the 2016 election. But the Musk trailer, which dropped Thursday, does not appear to fall in the category of the campaign advertising those bylaws were enacted to prevent. It simply contains a shot of a political rally in 2024 and a reference at the end to the 2024 election — the kind of flicks that occur in numerous documentaries and are hardly meant to stump for a particular candidate in an upcoming race.
The reason for YouTube’s rejection is even less clear, as the platform does allow campaign ads, albeit with “paid for” disclosures from vetted candidates.
Bleecker Street has entered an appeal with all three companies. Meta has already rejected the appeal. TikTok and YouTube are still entertaining the petitions. For its part, X has refused to engage with Bleecker Street on the film or even accept advertising for any of its other films on its upcoming calendar. Press reps at Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X did not immediately provide a comment. A Bleecker Street representative confirmed that the ads were initially rejected but said they are continuing to appeal with all three companies besides X in the hope minds can be changed.
Traction on social media is key for a documentary release, which relies on word-of-mouth in a way a big-budget feature doesn’t.
The news also hits a nerve after Universal, which is releasing the film overseas, considered backing away from distributing Musk before capitulating to public pressure and commenting that it is standing by the film (though no details have yet been given).
It is unclear if there has been any communication between ad reps at X and the other social giants. Some other tech firms will also see their leaders under the Hollywood spotlight this fall, with Sony releasing Aaron Sorkin’s Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning next month. That film’s trailer is currently available on YouTube.

U.S. equities rose on Friday as Wall Street wrapped up a volatile week of trading, with a surge in Treasury yields rippling through financial markets.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.51% to close at 7,743.41, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.5% to 27,068.72. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 478.64 points, or 0.93% to end at 51,828.62.
Akamai Technologies was a key winner of the session, rising 3% after announcing a multiyear deal with Anthropic .
Also helping sentiment, oil prices slid amid optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened, as Iran has asked the U.S. to return to the memorandum of understanding from June that failed to end the Middle East conflict. West Texas Intermediate crude futures dropped 2.33% to settle at $92.41 per barrel, while international benchmark Brent crude futures declined 2.14% to $104.32 a barrel.
With the day's gains, the Dow notched a winning week, up 0.3%. The S&P 500 added 1.2%, while the Nasdaq rose 2%.
That advance was bolstered by technology stocks such as Meta Platforms , which popped nearly 13% on the week amid excitement surrounding its artificial intelligence agent Muse . Information technology rose 3.1%, which was the most of any of the S&P 500's sectors.
The drama continued in the bond market, where the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2007 , while the 30-year yield reached its highest level since 2004. The two were last seen up slightly at 5.163% and 5.488%, respectively.
This week's ascent in yields was fueled by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, persistently high energy prices due to the Iran war, and a hot purchasing managers' report. Fed funds futures trading suggests a roughly 64% likelihood of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
Eric Diton, president of The Wealth Alliance, noted that investor sentiment has been weakening as bond yields have been rising, with bearish sentiment seeing a "sharp" increase from just two weeks earlier. That said, he believes the market has been "incredibly resilient" in the face of the developments, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq roughly 1% below their recent highs.
"Should rates continue to climb, they should have a larger impact on market performance at some point in the future," he cautioned.
Meanwhile, traders were monitoring Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the U.S. this week. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC Friday that " a lot more details " on negotiations between the U.S. and China are going to be released Monday.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier in the week that the two countries have agreed to extend their trade truce by two months.
The three leading U.S. indexes finished with gains on Friday.
The S&P 500 gained 0.51% to end the session at 7,743.41, while the Nasdaq Composite moved up 0.48% to 27,068.72. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 478.64 points, or 0.93%, to 51,828.62.
Wall Street can't agree on what's driving the surge in bond yields — whether it's stubborn inflation or rapid growth or the exploding deficit — but, whatever the cause, the likelihood that higher interest rates are here to stay is unnerving investors who fear that eventually something has to break .

The lavish black-tie affair in the historic East Room stands as one of the most star-studded evenings of the administration, offering a glitzy opportunity to smooth over notoriously fierce geopolitical friction with the superpower.
Trump heaped praise on Xi, whom he says he has developed a 'truly great friendship' with over his decade in politics .
However, the two nations remain divided on the war in Iran and are still grappling to find common ground on trade and how to best navigate the jarring advances of artificial intelligence .
During talks with Xi in Washington ahead of the dinner, the two sides discussed the Iran War, according to state broadcaster China Central Television.
Trump has argued to little effect that Beijing , which is far more dependent on Gulf oil than the US, has plenty of incentive to use its sway with Tehran to help force an end to the conflict.
But the President's war of choice has unnerved China, with the government condemning American and Israeli military action and Xi previously expressing concerns that the conflict signaled a return to what he called the 'law of the jungle.'

articles.title_orig: Presidents Cup: International team bounces back, sweeps foursomes matches to take lead at Medinah as U.S. struggles
articles.title_zh: Presidents Cup: International team bounces back, sweeps foursomes matches to take lead at Medinah as U.S. struggles
articles.content_orig:
Well, the International team bounced back.
The Americans struggled across the board on Friday at Medinah Country Club in Chicago, and will now have to enter the weekend at an event they've dominated since the beginning with plenty of work to do if they're going to retain the Presidents Cup.
The International team dominated on Friday to jump out of the early hole they found themselves in after Thursday's four-ball session. They won all five foursomes matches during the second day of play at the Presidents Cup, and now hold a 7-3 lead entering the weekend.
It was the seventh time that a team has swept a session in Presidents Cup history, and the first since the Internationals swept the foursomes session in 2024. The four-point lead also ties the largest lead the International team has held after two sessions, matching the 1998 event — the only one that the Americans have ever lost.
The U.S. team just couldn't get anything going, even with great looks from Wyndham Clark and Scottie Scheffler down the stretch. Now, over the last two Presidents Cups and Ryder Cups, the Americans are a combined 6-24-0 in foursomes matches, via Skratch's Dan Rapaport .
"They went out there and played great. They made a ton of putts," U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker said of the International team. "I feel like our guys hit a bunch of great putts and just couldn't find the bottom of the hole.
"You're going to have sessions like this in these things. I feel terrible for the guys because I know they grinded out there and gave me everything they had today, and it wasn't meant to be."
Hideki Matsuyama and Sungjae Im had the easiest time for the Internationals. After falling behind early, the duo carded three birdies in a four-hole stretch to suddenly take a three-hole lead through six in their matchup with Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman. One of those birdies even came after Im sank a putt from off the green.
They cruised to an easy 3&2 win to get a point on the board for the International team.
The International team was walking in putts throughout the course, too. Adam Scott drained a deep one himself early in his match alongside Christiaan Bezuidenhout, and the pair jumped to a three-hole lead at the turn while dominating Justin Thomas and Cameron Young. Thomas and Young didn't make a single birdie all day, and just looked off with each other throughout the round. Scott and Bezuidenhout won 3&2.
Then Ryan Fox walked one in too on the seventh with Min Woo Lee. Fox's birdie gave the International team the lead in four of the five matches at the time in a stunningly dominant start.
Si Woo Kim and Tom Kim erupted on the ninth green after a deep putt of their own, which gave them a two-shot lead at the turn over Patrick Cantlay and Xander Schauffele. They ended up taking a 4&3 win.
Scheffler and Sam Burns, who picked up their first international match play win together on Thursday, struggled to get past Corey Conners and Nick Taylor in the first group of the day. Scheffler had two great looks down the stretch to tie the match back up, and even had a golden opportunity at the 18th after Taylor sent his drive way off to the right of the fairway.
But Taylor stuck his approach to 2 feet after Conners pitched it out from behind the trees to save par, which sealed their 1-up win.
"It was more so redemption for that tee shot, but happy to walk away with a 4, and fortunate there that Sam's lipped out," Taylor said.
The only real bright side for the Americans came from Clark and Morikawa. Clark carried his pairing on Thursday to a win, and Morikawa managed five birdies together to keep pace with Fox and Lee. But Fox kept putting lights out, and walked in another long birdie at the 16th to put them back on top and eventually seal the 1-up win. That completed the five-match sweep, and gave the International team a four-point lead entering the weekend.
There is still a long way to go at Medinah. Saturday will feature a doubleheader with four-ball matches in the morning and foursomes matches in the afternoon before all 24 golfers will square off in singles matches on Sunday. But for now, the Americans have to make a significant move if they want to avoid being the first U.S. group to lose the cup in nearly two decades.
"This thing is 35, 40 percent over. It's not even halftime of a football game," Snedeker said. "There's a lot of golf left. … I'm fortunate to have these guys in the team room because I know what they're made of. I know what they're built of. It's going to be a long weekend, a lot of golf still left to play."

articles.title_zh: Unsecured OpenAI agents posted 53 user images on the internet without the lab's knowledge
articles.content_orig:
Disclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agents
Two ⁠months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.
The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to ⁠say when the images were posted.
The disclosure reveals a ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.
As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated ⁠that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activity and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.
OpenAI said its review would take “months” to complete given the scale of the work, and said it had notified “dozens” of third parties about improper activity.
Most of the leaked images have been ⁠taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.
OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for ​training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.
Before user posts are ‌used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out ‌metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.
But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might ‌leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.
In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or – just on Wednesday – by Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister, at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.
The 21 July announcement that OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by ​their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.
OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On 16 September, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain”.
Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers.
Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.
Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to ⁠include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.
Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that ​went unnoticed by the company for months.
Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives”.
In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement”. Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.
Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map
articles.content_orig:
People opposed to a congressional redistricting plan rally outside the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City, Mo., earlier this month. David A. Lieb/AP hide caption
In a case watched across the country and as voting begins in the midterm elections, the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map in Missouri that was aimed at netting Republicans another seat in the U.S. House.
This is the third time the high court has blocked the redistricting plan that could have helped ousted Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver by increasing the number of Republican voters in his district.
The court warned that changing maps now would cause "electoral chaos." The decision requires the state use the same districts provided to voters in 2022 and 2024. That's even though a different map was used in the primaries there last month.
It comes after weeks of conflicting rulings in state courts and federal courts. Elections officials in Missouri already started mailing some absentee ballots last week using the old districts and some argued it would be too late to change them.
Missouri lawmakers passed the new map last year at the behest of Trump. It was part of his nationwide strategy to draw more GOP-leaning seats to prevent Republicans from losing the House.
Usually, states redistrict at the start of each decade. The redistricting battle set off by Trump ended with the GOP besting the Democrats by tilting about nine or 10 more districts, including Missouri's fifth district , their way. Republicans currently only hold a few seats advantage in the House.
But opponents of the new Missouri map successfully gathered citizen signatures to put it to a vote on the November ballot.
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled earlier this month that the ballot question meant the 2025 GOP-backed map never went into effect and was never law – even though it had been used in the Aug. 4 primaries. The state's high court blamed Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for proceeding with the GOP map in the primaries even though it hadn't been approved by voters.
The U.S. Supreme Court in its ruling today backed that up, noting that the state court had said in May - before the primary - that the GOP map would require voter approval before it could be used.
The U.S. Supreme Court had declined on Sept. 10 to intervene in the state court's ruling but allowed the case to continue.
Simultaneously, Republicans sued in federal court and won backing for the GOP map from a federal judge and then, last week, a federal appeals court. That sent the case back to the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled against Republican lawmakers today.
In general, Republicans argued that their map should be used because more than a million Missourians cast votes in the primary using the map. Opponents of redistricting argued voters hadn't approved the map and blamed Republican officials for dragging out the process and of trying to force through the new map.

Akamai Technologies was a key winner of the session, rising 3% after announcing a multiyear deal with Anthropic .
Also helping sentiment, oil prices slid amid optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened, as Iran has asked the U.S. to return to the memorandum of understanding from June that failed to end the Middle East conflict. West Texas Intermediate crude futures dropped 2.33% to settle at $92.41 per barrel, while international benchmark Brent crude futures declined 2.14% to $104.32 a barrel.
With the day's gains, the Dow notched a winning week, up 0.3%. The S&P 500 added 1.2%, while the Nasdaq rose 2%.
That advance was bolstered by technology stocks such as Meta Platforms , which popped nearly 13% on the week amid excitement surrounding its artificial intelligence agent Muse . Information technology rose 3.1%, which was the most of any of the S&P 500's sectors.
The drama continued in the bond market, where the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2007 , while the 30-year yield reached its highest level since 2004. The two were last seen up slightly at 5.163% and 5.488%, respectively.
This week's ascent in yields was fueled by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, persistently high energy prices due to the Iran war, and a hot purchasing managers' report. Fed funds futures trading suggests a roughly 64% likelihood of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
Eric Diton, president of The Wealth Alliance, noted that investor sentiment has been weakening as bond yields have been rising, with bearish sentiment seeing a "sharp" increase from just two weeks earlier. That said, he believes the market has been "incredibly resilient" in the face of the developments, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq roughly 1% below their recent highs.
"Should rates continue to climb, they should have a larger impact on market performance at some point in the future," he cautioned.
Meanwhile, traders were monitoring Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the U.S. this week. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC Friday that " a lot more details " on negotiations between the U.S. and China are going to be released Monday.

articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo, a zig-zagging storm, threatens Hawaii with flooding rains

Hurricane Nolo is seen approaching Hawaii's islands, in this satellite image captured Friday. Nolo is expected to avoid making landfall as it strengthens, but forecasters warn it will bring dangerous flooding rains. NOAA/NESDIS/STAR/GOES-West hide caption
People on the Big Island of Hawaii are under a hurricane watch Friday afternoon, as Hurricane Nolo moves over the Pacific Ocean toward the Hawaiian archipelago. The alert means hurricane conditions are possible within 24 to 36 hours. By then, the storm will likely be a major hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
Nolo isn't expected to make landfall this weekend, but it has two dangerous qualities: slow movement and heavy rain . Maximum rainfall amounts from the storm in some areas could top 2 feet, forecasters say, with totals of 10 to 25 inches expected more widely.
"The time to finish preparations for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now," the NHC said in its public advisory. "Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible."
As of Friday afternoon, Nolo's maximum sustained winds were at 105 mph, making it a Category 2 storm, and it was moving at only 5 mph. It's now moving north-northeast and is expected to slow to a crawl before turning toward the west and picking up forward speed on Saturday and Sunday.
But it will continue to build strength from warm ocean waters. Over the next 72 hours, Nolo's winds could top out at 140 mph, according to the forecast discussion , making it a Category 4 storm.
A forecast cone shows the expected movements of Hurricane Nolo as it approaches the Hawaiian archipelago. NOAA/National Weather Service hide caption
The heaviest rains will likely fall on the Big Island's eastern and southern areas, forecasters say. Neighboring Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could see up to 10 inches of rain.
Hawaii and Maui counties have opened shelters to people and pets, according to Hawaii Public Radio , which also reports that schools and government offices began closing on Thursday in preparation for the storm.
Nolo's path over the water has been prone to sudden shifts. Earlier this week, it was heading west across open ocean when it took an abrupt right-hand turn, sending it north directly toward the Big Island.
The cyclone is the latest in a busy hurricane season in the Pacific, where warm water is feeding a powerful El Niño phenomenon that's sparking storms and reshaping weather patterns around the world. The Pacific region has already seen three Category 5 hurricanes: Genevieve, Lowell and Polo.
Nolo brings torrential rains to Hawaii weeks after the state endured flooding and wind damage from a series of natural disasters over this past year. In March, a winter storm system called a Kona low led to the worst flooding seen in Hawaii in over two decades. Then, in May, a 6.0 magnitude earthquake shook the Big Island.
In August, Hurricane Lala raked the Big Island, Maui, Oahu and Kauai at close range. And earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell pummeled Kauai and other areas.
Earlier this week, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said these four major disasters alone have damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes. He estimated recovery efforts will cost roughly $1 billion prior to Nolo.
"We will pursue every available federal resource, use insurance and state funding responsibly and work with the Legislature to protect our people and prepare Hawaiʻi for what comes next," he said in a press release .
Three hurricanes are spinning in the Pacific Ocean, as seen in this satellite image from Friday morning. In the west, Nolo is bringing rain to Hawaii while to the east, Hurricane Odalys grows over open water. Further east, the powerful Hurricane Polo is threatening Baja California Sur. hide caption
Nolo's growth represents a reversal: Last week, forecasters declared the system was dissipating and would not merit further updates unless it regenerated — and that's precisely what it did. Days ago, the NHC renewed issuing advisories of Tropical Depression Fifteen-E and warned that it could strengthen quickly. It then became Tropical Storm Nolo before intensifying into a hurricane.
Hurricane season in Hawaii typically runs through Nov. 30.

New Jersey’s Democratic lieutenant governor has stepped down following demands from the governor after an inquiry uncovered allegations of sexual harassment and ethical breaches related to his interactions with women.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill delivered an ultimatum to Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell requiring his departure by Friday, despite lacking the executive authority to oust him directly.
She confirmed his resignation during an afternoon press briefing.
"His decision will allow us to move forward with important work serving the people of our state," Sherrill stated. "In my administration we are committed to doing what is right, not what is politically expedient."
Sherrill selected Caldwell, a Methodist pastor and former president of Centenary University, to join her ticket last year.
The pair won election and assumed their roles in January, but an anonymous complaint regarding Caldwell's conduct toward women surfaced just four months into their term.
Because the lieutenant governor is independently elected in New Jersey, the governor cannot directly dismiss them.
However, the state Legislature holds the authority to impeach and remove a lieutenant governor, while a governor can strip the official of virtually all duties to effectively sideline them.
Sherrill commissioned an independent inquiry led by the law firm of Christopher Porrino, a former New Jersey attorney general.
The resulting report, published on Thursday, detailed multiple infractions of state protocol by Caldwell, 66.
Investigators found that he made unwanted advances toward a staff member’s friend, telling the employee after being rejected that "you young women are looking for young sperm."
Additionally, the report stated that Caldwell attempted to secure a job promotion for a state worker he was romantically involved with and invited personal guests to ticketed functions, including the opera, without paying for them as mandated by ethics guidelines.
Caldwell rejected the allegations. In a written response appended to the firm’s findings, he suggested his personal life was facing heightened scrutiny due to his status as a single Black man.
His attorney, Thomas Calcagni, asserted that Caldwell never made the remark about sperm nor leveraged his position to further his romantic life.
Calcagni acknowledged Caldwell recommended a female friend for advancement based solely on merit, maintaining he never demanded her promotion or intentionally breached ethics rules by failing to disclose their personal relationship when recommending her.
Sherrill maintained that Caldwell's departure was essential, pointing out he had engaged in "serious, repeated violations of state policy," even after receiving multiple warnings and training sessions.
Beyond being first in line to succeed the governor, Caldwell had served as New Jersey’s appointed secretary of state, giving him administrative oversight of state elections.
The political rift mirrors recent friction in neighboring New York, where Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul faced a bitter primary challenge from her estranged Lt. Gov. Antonio Delgado before he exited the race.
Hochul is seeking reelection this November alongside her new lieutenant governor nominee, Adrienne Adams, the former speaker of the New York City Council.

Donald Trump has attacked what he calls a “sick conspiracy” against AI after the head of Anthropic called for a slowdown in the technology’s development.
The US president warned that China would benefit after the bosses of Silicon Valley’s top AI companies backed calls to restrict AI development for safety reasons, calling the concerns a “hoax”.
He also launched a tirade against Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, whom he accused of trying to be a “perfect little angel”.
Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social: “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so!
“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”
Mr Amodei released a letter at the weekend calling for an industry-wide slowdown, endorsed by the US government, to prevent safety issues going “seriously wrong”.
In response, Mr Trump wrote: “Concerning AI, when, in the history of business, did anyone see the leaders of an industry call for regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy.
“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.”
JD Vance, the US vice-president, echoed Mr Trump’s comments, calling tech leaders’ requests a “Trojan horse”.
He added: “I have to say, just personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them.
“It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse.”
OpenAI has since called on the UK Government to introduce mandatory safety rules for major AI developers.
Under proposals supported by the company, the UK’s AI Security Institute would play a central role in third-party testing and creating adaptive technical standards.
Tom Duff-Gordon, the company’s head of policy in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told Politico: “OpenAI is in a position to support legislation in the UK to establish durable, mandatory, capability-based requirements for frontier AI that would build on the set of voluntary commitments that we currently have.”
Under the plans, Britain would move from the current system of voluntary agreements with AI companies to enforceable standards, bringing the UK in line with emerging frameworks in the EU and US.
The Government has not yet put forward plans for AI safety legislation, despite pressure from backbench MPs.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Wall Street after AI bosses called for a slowdown, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping by as much as 1.3pc.
Nvidia, the world’s largest listed company and a manufacturer of semiconductors used in the AI race, plunged by 4.2pc while fellow chipmaker AMD dropped 6.2pc.
The main European indexes in France, Germany and Spain were all down sharply on Monday after falls in South Korea and Japan overnight.

articles.content_orig:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned from his position following an investigation that found he violated state ethics and harassment policy , Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Friday at a press conference.
“He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted,” Sherrill said. Caldwell was not present at the announcement.
On Thursday, Sherrill urged Caldwell’s resignation after releasing a report summarizing the findings of a probe of his behavior conducted by a law firm hired by the state , which found evidence that he violated ethics rules by committing sexual harassment.
In a statement Thursday, Sherrill said that Caldwell, a fellow Democrat, “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.”
Caldwell’s resignation, she added, “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.”
Investigators said in the 61-page report that they found credible evidence that Caldwell violated workplace policy “in his conduct by commenting to a female staffer that young women want ‘young sperm.’”
They also found he violated an ethics code and code of conduct “when he brought guests to ticketed events without payment or reimbursement” and “when he sought to obtain a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship.”
Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.”
“This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Caldwell’s attorney Thomas Calcagni.
Calcagni didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.
On Friday, Sherrill pushed back on Calcagni’s criticism of the investigation, saying: “I think it’s very thorough. It lays out exactly what the investigation looked into.” She added that Caldwell’s own statements were included in the report, saying, “So, obviously he was fully involved in this as well.”
Sherrill also defended having Caldwell step in as acting governor on several occasions after the investigation began, saying, “As a former federal prosecutor, it is important to me that everyone have a fair hearing.”
“Once I saw those complaints, once I saw the findings of that investigation, I acted quickly and asked for the resignation of the lieutenant governor,” Sherrill said.
The governor said her demand that Caldwell step down is part of her efforts to dismantle a culture that ignores victims.
“There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug,” Sherrill said. “That is not the kind of government I’m running. When I say there is a culture change taking place, I mean it. This is part of it.”
New Jersey state Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin, a Democrat, applauded Sherrill for her “commitment to hold public officials to the highest standards.”
“Following an independent investigation, Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell was right to resign from office today,” Coughlin said in a statement. “We must ensure the work of governing is uninterrupted and that serving the people of New Jersey remains a top priority.”
Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, an office that oversees elections.
Sherrill said Friday that the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, would become acting secretary of state with just weeks to go until the midterm elections.
“Shirley is a veteran of the U.S. Department of Justice and the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office,” Sherrill said. “She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting.”
The lieutenant governor’s duties also include filling in for the governor when she leaves the state. Sherrill said that until a new lieutenant governor is in place, there is “an order of command” for who would step in for her during any absence, beginning with the state Senate president.
Under New Jersey law, the lieutenant governor must be replaced within 45 days of the position becoming vacant. Sherrill said she would “certainly” make a permanent appointment within that time frame but does not plan on naming an acting lieutenant governor in the meantime.
“We will be making sure with our chief counsel that we’re following the rules,” Sherrill said. “This is a little bit of a new area for New Jersey, so we’re going to ensure that we get legal opinions and follow the process there.”
Rebecca Shabad is a politics reporter for NBC News based in Washington.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', US media reports
articles.title_zh: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', US media reports
articles.content_orig:
The killing – which recalled lynchings – appeared to be over a drug dispute, authorities say, and two black men have been arrested
Investigators believe Tasia Fortune was already dead before the black woman’s body was hanged from a tree behind an abandoned home in the Mississippi capital this summer, a detective testified on Friday.
The hanging of Tasia Fortune’s body, which was found on August 3, was “staged”, Jackson police detective Samuel Dukes testified, citing the medical examiner’s opinion.
Authorities have not disclosed the exact cause of Fortune’s death, but they did rule it a homicide and have arrested two men, both of them black, on murder charges and issued a warrant for the arrest of a third person.
Dukes also testified that the motive for the killing appears to have been a drug dispute. He said interviews with others revealed that Fortune fought hard before she was killed.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift 'Cleveland!' lyrics detail Travis Kelce wedding
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift 'Cleveland!' lyrics detail Travis Kelce wedding
articles.content_orig:
Taylor Swift is tuning out the critics and celebrating married life with Travis Kelce in her new song " Cleveland! "
The pop superstar released the track Friday as one of four additions to "The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore," an expanded edition of her 2025 album. The project also includes the new songs "Patient Zero," "Pink Clouding" and "Babylon."
While the other tracks explore troubled relationships, fleeting euphoria and nostalgia, "Cleveland!" is a love song about Swift's husband and his Ohio roots. Kelce grew up in Cleveland Heights, and the song's title and lyrics appear to reference both his hometown and the "New Heights" podcast he hosts with his brother, Jason Kelce .
Swift sings about Kelce taking her to Cleveland and showing her the Heights before declaring him the "love of my life."
The song also contains what appears to be a reference to Swift and Kelce's wedding. In its final chorus, Swift changes the wording to note that "now I'm wearing white," seemingly nodding to the couple ' s July 3 nuptials at Madison Square Garden in New York City.
The lyric goes: "He already took me to Cleveland, now I'm wearing white / So hate all you like, this is the love of my life."
The wedding reference arrives after Swift spends much of the track confronting the scrutiny that has followed her public life and relationship. She revisits familiar criticism about her appearance, fashion choices and dancing before making it clear that Kelce's opinion matters more to her than outside commentary.
"And with all of that money, why's she dressed like trash? / When she smiles, it's annoying, and have you seen her? / Stumbling clumsily? Would you even call that dancing?" she sings. "The taste of me is acquired, but it's his favorite dish / He says I look like an angel, they say, 'I hate that b****' / There, that house with the porch is where he lived as a kid."
Swift and Kelce began dating in 2023 and the couple announced their engagement in August 2025 and married the following summer.
"Cleveland!" is among Swift's first new musical releases since the wedding. "The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore" follows the original album's October release and adds four tracks to its lineup nearly one year later.
Swift announced the expanded edition Sept. 23 on Instagram, saying the additional music was inspired by fans’ enthusiasm for the original album.
The four new songs are available digitally now.

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday after a federal judge ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore their press access.
The re-entry came after a chaotic morning, during which the three outlets filed an emergency request for a hearing, accusing the Trump Administration of having “repeatedly violated” the court order and refusing several reporters access to the White House grounds. "This morning, journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in the court document.
Judge Timothy Kelly had given the Trump Administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond to the outlets' filing.
In a court filing of its own, the White House said it "began the process" of reinstating press badges shortly at 7:25 a.m. ET and laid out a timeline of what followed. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Early Thursday, in a District of Columbia court, Judge Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” He ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ​ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning .
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge over the ban and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted : “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
“Either the preliminary injunction will be issued or denied,” says Eugene Volokh, a law professor at UCLA who specializes in the First Amendment. “The temporary restraining order would then lapse, and whichever side loses can then appeal to the D.C. Circuit.”
Instead of an appeal, Trump could file for emergency relief from the D.C. court, similar to how CNN, MS NOW, and Politico did Thursday, according to experts.
But “emergency relief is usually harder to get than a resolution through appeal,” says Volokh.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.
Volokh says that legal precedent in the D.C. Circuit, used in both the ongoing case and that of Acosta, has “already been set” for areas of the White House usually open to the media, including the press briefing room.
“The government can't exclude reporters based on viewpoint, and cannot take away a press pass without due process, without some sort of hearing opportunity to be heard, an explanation of what it is that they supposedly did wrong, what rules they violated,” he says.
In light of this, an appeal from the Trump Administration after a preliminary injunction would likely be rejected in the D.C. Circuit, he argues. However, the President may find a better chance in the Supreme Court.
“Generally speaking, the First Amendment does not secure a right of access to government office buildings,” says Volokh, once again noting the exception of areas usually granted access for press. "The same position could be taken by the Supreme Court, and [it] might say: 'Look, the government can pick and choose whom to allow on its property,'" he says.
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said : “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post —announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi end summit with tea, tour of US archives - and little sign of progress
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi end summit with tea, tour of US archives - and little sign of progress
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_orig: Coca-Cola hires Rob Gehring from Monster Energy to run its North American operations
articles.title_zh: Coca-Cola hires Rob Gehring from Monster Energy to run its North American operations
articles.content_orig:
Rob Gehring, the head of Monster Energy 's Americas business, will leave to run Coca-Cola 's North America unit, the companies said Friday.
He will take over the position on Dec. 1.
The move comes as Coke tries to maintain growth while U.S. consumers cut back on spending in the face of higher gas and grocery prices. Despite those dynamics, the beverage giant posted net sales growth of 7% in the second quarter, as volume — a key measure of demand — rose 3% in North America.
Though Monster Energy parent Monster Beverage is considerably smaller than Coke, its sales have soared in part due to innovation in the energy drink space. The company reported net sales growth of 20% in its second quarter.
Coke is also investing in developing new beverages beyond its core soda offerings, including refreshers and dirty sodas.
Gehring, 59, took on his previous role at Monster in February after serving as chief growth officer since 2024. In a press release, Coke said he was "part of the leadership team that drove the company's growth agenda and modernized commercial capabilities."
Before joining Monster, Gehring was CEO of Swire Coca-Cola USA, a major bottler of Coke products in the western U.S.
Coke shares have climbed more than 25% this year, while Monster's stock has risen more than 12%.

articles.title_orig: Government can use Social Security data to identify noncitizen voters, Supreme Court rules
articles.title_zh: Government can use Social Security data to identify noncitizen voters, Supreme Court rules
articles.content_orig:
The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens.
Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could  result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls.
In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibits broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, which limits any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms.
But states can still check the citizenship of individual voters.
The three liberal-leaning justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the majority decision.
One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters.
"The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save), allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.
The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits.
But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls.
In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote".
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.
The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies, and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information.
The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary.
The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task".
Voting rights groups called the ruling "profoundly disappointing".
"...it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections," the League of Women Voters, the lead plaintiff in the case, said in a statement.
"We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans' voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands," it said.
Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship.
Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes.
For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports.
Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas.
Some states, like Georgia, have worked with the government on the Save programme.
Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, has touted his office's work with the programme and his recommendations to improve the system.
Raffensperger told the BBC his office thoroughly vetted the government-provided data  to determine whether flagged individuals were non-citizens, even interviewsing some of the voters in question to ensure accuracy.
"There's always guardrails in place, to make sure that we never denied the right to vote," Raffensperger said.
Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to reign in mail-in ballots.
In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters.
The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls.
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.
